1:
The four conditional clauses are not doubts. Clarke says the particle expresses no hesitation but is a strong affirmation, as there is consolation in Christ and as there is comfort of love, and Robertson notes that all four conditions are of the class that assumes the thing to be true. What the first word means is less settled. Gill entertains both senses, an exhortation made in the name of Christ and a consolation to be had from him; Clarke reports that several critics prefer the first; Calvin sets the exhortation reading out fully and then rejects it as answering the context less well than consolation; Ellicott takes it as encouragement, the stirring up of spiritual activity, and Robertson renders it a ground of appeal. Ellicott then reads the verse as a double pair, the first two clauses tracing a spiritual effect to union with Christ and the second two tracing another to communion with the Spirit, and observes that the one is shown in action visibly following the divine example while the other is inward emotion, not seen but felt. Robertson notes that the fourth clause does not agree in gender and number, and passes on the conjecture that an early copyist, or even the man taking the letter down, wrote one form for another.

Chrysostom frames the whole appeal as a father's. There is nothing more affectionate than a spiritual teacher, he says, who surpasses the kindness of any natural father, and he puts the words into a father's mouth: if you have any reverence for me, any memory of my care in nourishing you, any of my kindness, then be not at enmity with your brother, and for all those things this is what I ask in return. Calvin notices precisely the opposite about the manner, that the apostle humbles himself by beseechingly imploring their pity when he might have used his paternal authority and demanded the respect due to him from his sons; and he gives the reason for the urgency, that torn by intestine contentions they would lie open to the impostures of false apostles, since disagreement always opens a door for Satan to spread impious doctrine, while agreement is the best bulwark against it.

On the request itself Gill lists the grounds of the joy already had, their steadfastness under persecution and the fresh instance of their love in sending their minister to him with a present; Calvin marvels that a man shut up in prison and in view of the executioner should have unmingled joy provided the churches were in good condition, and says the Philippians would have been worse than cruel to torture him with a second anguish. Where the four terms of the second verse divide them is in the order of unity. Henry holds that Christians should be one in affection whether they can be one in apprehension or not, since affection is always in their power and is the likeliest way to bring them nearer in judgment; Calvin puts it the other way, that the beginning of love is harmony of views, though that is not enough unless hearts are joined in affection too; Barnes wishes perfect unity of sentiment and plan were attainable and settles for as much as will prevent discord, adding that there is probably no single thing so much insisted on in the New Testament as harmony among Christians and almost nothing so little known. Ellicott traces a rising gradation to a union of soul in which each sinks his individuality in a common love, and Robertson finds his images in souls that beat together and clocks that strike at the same moment. Wesley distributes the clauses among the three Persons, the same thought because Christ is the common Head, the same love because God is the common Father, one soul because all have drunk into one Spirit.
3:
Calvin names the two pests: contention, awakened whenever a man is prepared to maintain his own opinion pertinaciously and rushing headlong once it has begun, and vainglory in those whose object is power and who are offended at seeing others above them; ambition, he says, is the bellows that kindles all strifes, and for both diseases there is one remedy, humility, the mother of moderation. Barnes turns the prohibition into a catalogue of the ways it is broken, denominations outstripping one another, ministers preaching with no better aim, competition in dress and equipage, and even plans of benevolence pursued with the secret aim of outdoing others, against all of which he sets that the Redeemer never once acted from such a motive. Gill enters the necessary qualification, that they were not forbidden all striving, since they were to strive for the faith of the gospel and the purity of its ordinances, but only striving to carry a point without regard to reason or to the infirmities of the weak. Robertson notes that the word for lowliness of mind is late and rare, absent from the older writers and used in a bad sense for pusillanimity by Josephus and Epictetus, and calls it one of the words Christianity has ennobled.

What esteeming others better amounts to divides them. Ellicott denies that moral superiority is in view at all: the neighbour is to be held worthy of higher consideration and a higher place of dignity, so that self-assertion is entirely overborne. Clarke and Wesley ground the estimate instead in self-knowledge, since every man knows more evil of himself than he can know of another, and charity therefore supposes his brethren more holy and more devoted than he is, while they think the same of him, their own secret defects being known only to themselves. Robertson renders the participle neutrally as excelling.

The next command is guarded by three voices in three different directions. Ellicott protects it from being pressed into a denial of all self-love, which he thinks a fault of some modern speculation, since a man is individual as well as social and may subordinate his own things without ignoring them; he also holds that looking upon is more than seeking, expressing the insight into another's thoughts and hopes that only a self-forgetting love can give. Barnes guards it the other way, that we are not to pry into the purposes of others or obtrude advice unsought, nothing being more odious than an intermeddler. Gill guards it in a third way, that a man must still provide for his own household or be worse than an infidel, and refers the command chiefly to spiritual gifts and the peace of the church; Clarke reads it likewise of not arrogating to ourselves the gifts that belong to others, and of rejoicing when God uses another to much effect.

Then the example is produced. Chrysostom observes that the Lord set before his disciples himself, the Father and the prophets, and that the apostle follows the same method here and elsewhere, giving the reason: nothing rouses a great soul to good works so much as learning that in them it is likened to God, and no encouragement is equal to that. Calvin divides the appeal in two, that imitation of Christ is the rule of right living and also the road by which true glory is attained, and notes that he has kept the passive form of the verb without disapproving the other rendering. Henry states the principle plainly, that we must resemble him in his life if we would have the benefit of his death. Barnes points to the distance travelled, from a state of inexpressible glory to the most lowly offices, and Gill to the whole descent as far as the death of the cross; Robertson says simply that humility is urged as the only way to secure unity.
6:
What the form of God is divides the commentary down the middle, and not along the usual lines. Clarke argues from the structure of the sentence: whatever it was, he divested himself of it, so it can be neither the divine nature, which he could not lay aside, nor the government of the world, nor the power of working miracles, which he kept all through his ministry; the word signifies external appearance and not nature or essence, and he concludes for the visible glorious light in which the Deity is said to dwell. Calvin lands in much the same place by another road: the word means majesty, and as a man is known by the look of his face, so the majesty shining forth in God is his form; better still, it is the insignia by which a king is recognised, his sceptre and crown and mantle. Ellicott takes the contrary view flatly, that in classical Greek the word describes the specific character which makes each being what it is, so that the clause asserts essential and therefore eternal being in the true nature of God; Robertson calls it a clear statement of the deity of Christ, and Wesley renders it the incommunicable nature, which puts him on the opposite side from Clarke. Barnes lays out both possibilities at length without forcing the choice. Wesley notes that the word for equal, wherever else it occurs, expresses not a bare resemblance but a real and proper equality, and Robertson that the prize was one to be held on to rather than something to be seized.

Of what, then, was he emptied? Gill, Barnes and Calvin all insist that nothing whatever was lost. Gill says he took what he had not before without losing anything he had, the glory of his divine nature being covered and out of sight; Barnes offers the figure of the sun obscured by cloud, whose beams are not extinguished and whose glory is not really changed; Calvin says he laid aside his glory in the view of men not by lessening it but by concealing it, the abasement of the flesh serving as a veil. Ellicott identifies the glory laid down with that which he had with the Father before the world was, and notes that it was resumed for a moment at the transfiguration and worn anew at the ascension. Wesley goes further than any of them, saying that he not only veiled but in some sense renounced that glory. Robertson, naming the controversy, allows real limitations of space and knowledge and power while urging restraint, denies any limitation by error, and passes on the phrase that he stripped himself of the insignia of majesty. Calvin also raises the question whether the emptying belongs to the manhood only, reports that Erasmus answered yes, objects that the form of God was there before he became man, and answers that the apostle speaks of Christ entire while the thing applies to one nature, as when we call man mortal and mean his body.

On the two clauses that follow, Ellicott distinguishes the word for form from the word for fashion, the one the actual nature and the other the outward appearance, and observes that the likeness of men means men as they actually are, so that the humiliation went beyond assuming humanity to seeming one of the multitude, in a station that confused him with the commoner sort. Robertson insists the likeness was a real one and no phantom humanity such as the Docetists held, and marks the change of tense from eternal existing to a definite entrance in time. Cyril of Jerusalem puts the clause to a use of his own, comforting the poor and the enslaved before the judgment seat: he who took the form of a servant does not despise servants.
8:
Robertson distinguishes the third term from the two before it as what he was in the eyes of men rather than what he was in himself, and calls the cross the bottom rung of the ladder from the throne of God; Barnes takes it of state or condition. Gill guards the word from the docetic sense, that the particle here denotes not mere likeness but the thing itself. Clarke numbers five steps of the descent, ending with the death of the cross, and breaks off to ask what sin must be in the sight of God when it required such abasement to make an atonement for it. Here Ellicott dissents sharply: the death is not regarded in this passage as an atonement, for in that light it could be no pattern to us, but as the completion of the obedience of a whole life. Calvin says that by dying so he was accursed in the sight of God, and Cyril of Jerusalem states the substitution at length, that God must either destroy all men in his truth or cancel the sentence in his loving-kindness, and preserved both.

On the exaltation Calvin turns aside to protest against those who seize the word wherefore to prove that Christ merited first for himself and afterwards for others, which he calls a suggestion of Satan obscuring the grace of Christ. Barnes refers the exaltation to the Redeemer as sustaining both natures; Robertson asks what glory Christ had after the ascension that he had not before, and what he carried back that he had not brought, and answers that it was his humanity, so that he returned as Son of Man as well as Son of God; Clarke says no creature is so exalted as the man Christ Jesus, human nature being dignified beyond the angelic. What the name is they do not agree. Robertson takes it naturally for the name Jesus, given in the verse following, while listing the alternatives; Ellicott takes it for the Name of God, properly Jehovah, confirming this from the adoration that follows, claimed in the prophet as the sole due of God; Wesley and Barnes keep to dignity and majesty above every creature; Clarke notes the article read by good authorities.

Whether the verse warrants bowing at the sound of the name is answered with some heat. Barnes denies it flatly, observing that the custom in some churches has arisen entirely from a misinterpretation, and that if such homage were meant it would be the knee and not the head. Gill agrees and presses further, that the name was common among the Jews, so the bare sound commands no peculiar respect, and that several creatures named have no knees; he would render the phrase in the name rather than at it. Robertson calls it no matter of perfunctory genuflection, and Ellicott observes that in the name is the standing expression for worship offered to God, denoting worship paid to Christ and not through him. Calvin, insisting on outward profession as well as inward affection, asks whether the adoration belongs to the divinity or the humanity, answers that neither alone will serve, and refers it to the entire person. On the third class named, Clarke takes it of those in the shades below who died without receiving salvation, or else of fallen spirits; Gill names angels, departed souls and devils together; Robertson gives the word as the old adjective for the departed, simply the dead; Wesley takes the three as the whole universe, bowing either with love or with trembling.
12:
Chrysostom draws a rule of pastoral method from the opening: admonitions ought to be accompanied with commendations, so that those admonished are told it is not other men but their own selves they are bidden to take for an example. He and Calvin agree about the clause on absence. Chrysostom hears the apostle saying that what was done under his eye might have been done out of respect and shame, and that doing more now proves it was done for God's sake; Calvin adds that it is the part of hypocrites to approve themselves before others and indulge themselves once withdrawn from public view, so that when the monitor is at a distance they must stir up themselves. Ellicott notes in passing that this is the only epistle containing no direct rebuke. On the verb Henry presses that it means working thoroughly and taking true pains, not doing something now and then but doing all that is to be done and persevering to the end; Ellicott makes it carrying to completion what God has begun, man's co-operation being secondary and intermediate; Wesley observes with some point that here, and only here, each man is to aim at his own things, and Henry that though we must promote the common salvation we may on no account neglect our own.

How hard the fear is meant to be they do not agree. Chrysostom takes the second word for an excessive degree of fear, notes that Paul himself had it, and asks who ever learnt even his letters without fear. Clarke refers it to the difficulty of the work and the danger of miscarriage; Henry likewise makes it trembling lest they come short, and calls fear a great guard and preservative from evil. Robertson passes on two milder glosses, that it is not slavish terror but wholesome serious caution, and that it is a nervous anxiety to do right; Ellicott relates the phrase instead to the reverence of a servant toward a superior and to the willingness to suffer shown in the obedience of Christ.

The reason given raises the whole question, and the voices divide as sharply as anywhere in the chapter. Clarke states a formula: God gives the power to will and man wills through it, God gives the power to act and man acts through it, so that God neither wills for man nor works in his stead, and the use of those powers belongs to man, who is accountable for them. Calvin takes the contrary ground, that any action has two departments, the inclination and the power to carry it into effect, and that both are ascribed here wholly to God, leaving us nothing as a ground of glorying; he attacks the schoolmen who would give free will a separate power to co-operate with grace, and calls the verse the sword that puts an end to all pride. Gill agrees, adding that the grace works efficaciously and not by moral persuasion. Barnes holds a middle line by negatives, stating the objection plainly, that if God does all the work we might sit still, and answering that God does not act for us and does not compel us against our will, but leads us to will. Ellicott calls it a famous paradox whose two terms are recognised by our deepest consciousness and irreconcilable to our logic, and observes that Scripture brings out each in turn and leaves the reconcilement untouched. Robertson says the same more sharply, that the apostle exhorts like an Arminian when addressing men and prays like a Calvinist when addressing God, and feels no inconsistency in the two attitudes. Wesley divides the verse itself: the first clause is our duty, the second our encouragement.
14:
Ellicott separates the two faults carefully: the second word is used mostly of cavils and objections in speech and indicates intellectual questioning, while the first denotes the outward wrangling of discontent and proceeds from the heart rather than the mind; he thinks the precept is left in deliberate generality, though the example set before men inclines him to refer it primarily to their dealings with each other. Robertson notes that the word for murmuring is a late one formed in imitation of the sound, and that the grumblings led on to the disputes. Calvin reads the pair as secret enmity first and open contention after, tracing both to a man who aims beyond measure at his own advantage. Henry puts it most bluntly, that God's commands were given to be obeyed and not disputed, and adds that the light of truth and the life of religion are often lost in the heats and mists of disputation. Barnes ties the verse back to the earlier charge of humility, and Wesley calls murmuring and disputing real though smaller hindrances of love.

Gill finds an active as well as a passive sense in being blameless: not only that no one should have just cause to blame them, but that they should be without blaming others, some men being so unhappy in disposition as to find fault with all persons and things they have to do with. Ellicott distinguishes blamelessness before external law and judgment from the inward purity and simplicity of the second word, and reports that the best manuscripts give a third term meaning unblemished; Barnes takes that word as properly meaning unmixed, and so artless and without guile; Wesley divides them, blameless before men and simple before God. Calvin grants that such perfection has never existed in the world and calls those blameless who aim at it with the whole bent of the mind, adding that adoption itself ought to be a motive. To whom the crooked and perverse generation refers they do not agree. Barnes thinks it not improbable that those particularly meant were the Jews at Philippi, since the phrase is taken from the song of Moses, and Clarke says the same; Wesley applies it instead to the bulk of mankind, crooked by a corrupt nature and more perverse by custom and practice; Calvin describes only believers intermingled with unbelievers on every side, and Ellicott traces the wording to the same passage of Moses without narrowing its application.

The figure at the close is construed four ways. Ellicott keeps to the luminaries, which hold forth their light, and declines the torch-race image as an unnecessary change of metaphor, observing that Christians are the lesser lights of heaven, dim beside the Sun of Righteousness and seen only in the night of this life. Clarke introduces something quite different, the fires kept burning on towers at harbour mouths to guide ships in, and carries it into the next clause as a weather-beaten mariner brought safe to port at last. Calvin makes us lamps carrying the wick from which the light comes, or else candlesticks bearing the candle of the doctrine, and warns that we do the word an injustice if it does not shine out of us in purity of life. Robertson doubts any connection with the preceding figure and thinks the context calls for holding fast rather than holding forth. Barnes leaves the metaphor aside for the duty, that Christians are kept on earth for this purpose and would otherwise be removed to heaven at once on conversion, and that there is nobody else to do it. Gill takes the word of life either of Christ himself or of the gospel that quickens.
17:
The figure is a libation, and where it is drawn from is disputed. Barnes explains it from the drink-offering poured on the altar before the offerer tasted it, and thinks the apostle regarded himself as a victim prepared for sacrifice. Clarke carries forward the metaphor he had begun at the previous verse: as the weather-beaten mariner on gaining port would sacrifice the animal he had vowed while in danger, so the apostle, having guided them safely in, was willing that his own blood should be the libation poured upon that offering. Ellicott notes that such a libation was reckoned a subsidiary element of the offering, and draws the consequence that the martyrdom is valued not for itself but as conducing to their own self-sacrifice by faith, contemplated as offered in life rather than in death. Calvin derives the word quite differently, from the victims by which treaties were confirmed among the ancients, so that the apostle calls his death the confirmation of their faith; and he shifts the parts, making the apostle the priest who had offered them to God by the gospel, their faith being the oblation. Robertson declares it uncertain whether heathen or Jewish offerings are in view and holds the question unimportant.

On the call to rejoice Barnes tells a story from antiquity that answers exactly to the two verbs: an Athenian returned from Marathon bleeding and exhausted, rushed in before the magistrates, uttered only the words rejoice, we rejoice, and died on the spot. Ellicott takes the occasion for a longer reflection, that joy is natural in the first thoughts of childhood, chequered or destroyed by the second thoughts of fuller experience, and comes back in the third and deepest thoughts of the Christian, solemnised but deepened into thankfulness, so that a Christianity with no power to rejoice may be true but is imperfect. Calvin says the apostle's alacrity was meant to enkindle them to meet death with firmness, and that though losing such a teacher was a serious loss it was no slight compensation that the gospel was confirmed by his blood. Gill adds that they should not indulge sorrow at the news, and Wesley reduces the whole to two words.

Chrysostom asks the sharp question about the mission that follows: why does he not say that you may know my state, but that I may know yours? Because Epaphroditus would have reported his own state before Timothy could arrive; and he notes how everything, even the sending of a messenger, is referred to Christ. Calvin gives another reason, that as the expectation of help animates soldiers in war, so looking for Timothy would keep them from giving way to impostors, and he presses the condition attached, since nothing may be determined about the future except under the Lord's hand; Gill makes the same point negatively, that the trust was not in an arm of flesh nor in princes. Barnes observes that Timothy's earlier presence at Philippi is nowhere stated in the history though the narrative makes it probable, and that the offhand way the fact is mentioned here is such as would occur to no one composing a forgery. Ellicott notes that Timothy is spoken of here in the third person, so that although he is joined in the salutation the letter is the apostle's alone, and hears in the words some anxiety but more confidence. Henry observes that though he was himself a great apostle he took all occasions to speak with respect of those far his inferiors, and Clarke and Robertson add that the good cheer waited on the news.
20:
Whom Timothy is said to resemble is a question of grammar with some weight. Robertson insists the adjective means likeminded with Timothy and not with the apostle, so that the claim is that no one else is his equal; Calvin reads it the same way, that the comparison is with the others rather than with Paul himself, and that the eulogium was pronounced so that Timothy might be the more esteemed. Gill and Ellicott take it the other way, that he had a soul like the apostle's own, Gill saying they had as it were but one soul in two bodies and Ellicott recalling that Paul elsewhere calls him a true son in the faith. On the adverb Barnes gives sincerely, Ellicott genuinely, without counterfeit or duplicity of aim, and Robertson traces the word to legitimate rather than spurious birth.

The saying that all seek their own is felt by every voice to be hard, and each softens or resolves it differently. Wesley alone takes it at full strength and exclaims that in that golden age of the church only one of all the labourers with him could be thoroughly approved, asking how many now could approve themselves to God. Gill restricts it to the greatest part rather than every individual. Clarke confines it to those who preached of envy and strife, allowing that even men of good will might be unfit for so demanding an errand. Calvin denies that they were intent exclusively on their own interests, and says only that, being taken up with them, they were to some extent negligent of the public advantage; but he adds that it is impossible for a man devoted to self to apply himself to the interests of the church, which is why such a fault renders its subjects useless. Ellicott calls the declaration startling, contrasts the scanty notice of companions at the close of this letter with the detailed and affectionate lists in others, and suggests either an accidental separation from his trusty disciples or a temporary falling away. Robertson disposes of the difficulty another way, by observing that Luke must have been away from Rome at that juncture. Barnes asks only that we should not judge them harshly.

On the commendation that follows Ellicott notices that the construction is curiously broken: it begins as a son to a father, as though the dutiful ministration of Timothy were to be described, and then changes, in a characteristic humility, to make the two merely fellow-servants. Clarke and Robertson press the same point from the preposition, that Timothy did not serve the apostle but served with him, and Clarke adds that in those times there were no sinecures, apostles and bishops labouring as hard as their deacons, every man a labourer and every labourer with his wages. Calvin fastens instead on the modesty this implies, and complains that the virtue has been rare in every age, since one may look in vain among the young for anyone who will give way to his seniors in the smallest thing. Barnes and Robertson take the proof as the testing of a metal, and the voices differ slightly on how often the Philippians had seen him, Ellicott counting four occasions from the history and Robertson three. On the delay, Barnes and Clarke explain that the trial was approaching and its issue doubtful, and Calvin that although deliverance was expected there was no express promise, so that the expectation hung suspended on the secret purpose of God; Ellicott and Robertson both insist that the phrase in the Lord is no formality but belongs to a life that cannot hope except in Christ.
25:
The three titles are read as a rising scale. Ellicott makes them brother in a common Christianity, fellow-worker in the service of Christ, and fellow-soldier in the daring the warfare of the cross implies; Robertson notes that a single article covers all three and marks the ascent from common sympathy to common work to common danger; Calvin dwells on the last, that the term declares the condition of the ministers of the gospel, who are engaged in an incessant warfare, so that those preparing to edify the church should know that war is declared against them. On the fourth title Ellicott reports and rejects the view, held by interpreters ancient and modern, that the word designates the chief pastor of the Philippian church, since no example confirms such a use; Robertson takes it simply as messenger, and Wesley refers it to the errand of carrying their contribution. Three voices decline identifications: Ellicott calls it extremely precarious to identify him with the Epaphras of another epistle, since a native Colossian would hardly be the chosen messenger of Philippi, Robertson says flatly they are not the same man, and Gill notes that a freedman of Nero bore the name at Rome in those years.

The sickness draws a long argument. Clarke quotes at length the observation that no miracle is intimated, the recovery being spoken of as natural, and that this proves the power of working cures visited the apostles only occasionally and did not depend on their own will, since Paul would certainly have healed him if he could; a forgery, it is added, would not have spared a miracle here. Barnes reports the same argument from the same source. Ellicott arrives independently at the same conclusion, and adds that an apostle could not, as our Lord would not, work miracles for his own needs. Calvin raises a different difficulty and presses it hard: how can a lengthened life be called a mercy of God, when the apostle had shortly before declared that he desired death in preference to life? Gill observes that good men whom Christ loves are still sick, and Robertson traces the word for the messenger's distress either to homesickness or to bewilderment.

Ellicott finds a peculiar pathos in the phrase about being less sorrowful: the recovery would remove the sorrow upon sorrow, but the old sorrow of captivity and enforced inactivity would remain, so that the profession of perfect joy belongs to the willing spirit while the hint of an unspoken sorrow marks the weakness of the flesh. Calvin turns the charge to receive him into a rule about pastors, that they are precious pearls from God's treasuries, the rarer the more to be esteemed. The last verse carries a textual crux. Barnes sets out both readings, the received one meaning not taking pains and the other exposing oneself to danger, and judges the second to suit the connection; Clarke names the manuscripts and reports it received into the text; Ellicott renders it having gambled with his life, not merely staked but staked recklessly, and reports though doubts a suggestion that it alludes to the caution money forfeited in a lawsuit; Robertson cites an inscription for the sense and adds that the cognate word was afterwards applied to those Christians who risked their lives for the dying and the dead. On the closing words Ellicott, Barnes, Calvin and Wesley agree that no reproach is intended, the Philippians being simply at a distance and unable to serve in person.
